title: Is the Senate's READ Act a Reading First Redux?
author: Mike Petrilli
summary: Mike Petrilli, education policy analyst and president of the Thomas B. Fordham Institute, evaluates the Senate's proposed READ Act and questions whether federal intervention is necessary or wise given that over 40 states have already enacted science-of-reading reforms independently. The article is framed by Petrilli's 'Reading First PTSD' — reference to the 2001-era federal literacy program that imposed prescriptive requirements with mixed results. He describes the READ Act's provisions (modifying the CLSD grant program, requiring teacher prep alignment with science of reading, mandating early literacy screening) and notes two scenarios: it could be a well-intentioned but unnecessary nudge to the few remaining holdout states, or it could import the same problems Reading First encountered by centralizing pedagogical mandates at the federal level. Petrilli's deeper concern is the rhetoric-to-substance gap: a stirring call to action from advocates like Keri Rodrigues of the National Parents Union does not automatically translate into a bill with sufficient teeth or precision to close the gap between the science-of-reading movement's promise and its implementation realities.
points: With over 40 states having already enacted science-of-reading reforms on their own, the most important question about the READ Act is whether federal mandates add meaningful leverage over holdout states or merely arrive late to a parade states are already leading.

Petrilli's 'Reading First PTSD' is a substantive reference: the 2001-era federal literacy program generated implementation problems, political backlash, and mixed evidence — cautionary precedent for any federal attempt to define what reading instruction must look like at the classroom level.

The bill rewards low-performing states with better access to existing grant funds — a 'Race to the Bottom' structure that Petrilli finds conceptually odd when the goal is to incentivize improvement rather than label and fund failure.

The gap between accountability-focused reformers like Petrilli and scholars like Ross Wiener — who has argued that NCLB-era accountability transferred 'moral commitment to standardized tests' — reflects a deep disagreement about whether objective measures serve equity or distort education.

What matters most for science-of-reading implementation, Petrilli argues, is not whether a federal law passes but whether the policies are implemented faithfully and with quality at the school level — a question the bill does not definitively answer.
quotes: 'The wake-up call is here. Wake up, wake the hell up. How many times do you have to be called to action? How many panel discussions do we have? How many congressional briefings, congressional hearings, all of this stuff? We all know what the problem is. Let's get together and solve it.' — Keri Rodrigues
That's quite a stirring introduction to a federal bill that, to my eyes, doesn't do much, isn't really needed, and could possibly do harm. But maybe that's just my Reading First PTSD speaking.

One possibility is that this bill is a nothing-burger. If all it does is tweak an existing grant program (the CLSD), maybe it's fine. I find it a little weird that we'd reward low-performing states with a better chance at winning the money (Race to the Bottom, anyone?), but OK, whatever.

Over 40 states have enacted science-of-reading reforms already; what's the case for Uncle Sam trying to jump out and lead this parade? Perhaps this bill would encourage a few states to embrace more comprehensive reforms than they otherwise would.
We already know that what really matters (on this issue, like most) is whether the policies are implemented faithfully and with quality.
